planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or early fall; stem cuttings root readily in water or moist perlite within 3-4 weeks.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where trailing stems root as they travel to form a dense evergreen mat. Needlepoint carries narrow, deeply cut five-lobed leaves with elongated pointed tips, giving a finer, more delicate texture than broad-leaved English ivy types and making it a long-favored choice for topiary, wreaths, and hanging baskets as well as groundcover. Like the species, it is considered invasive across much of the eastern United States and Pacific Northwest, where it escapes cultivation and smothers native woodland understory; check local regulations before planting outdoors. Shear back hard every few years to remove woody growth and keep the foliage dense and juvenile.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or early fall; this cultivar tolerates colder planting-season temperatures than most English ivy selections.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where trailing stems root as they spread into a dense, weed-smothering evergreen mat. Thorndale was selected for outstanding cold hardiness and is among the most reliable English ivy cultivars for northern climates, with glossy, medium-sized dark green leaves showing light silvery veining that take on a bronzed cast in cold winter weather. It is a vigorous grower well suited to large-scale bank and slope plantings but, like the species, is classified as invasive in much of the eastern United States and parts of the Pacific Northwest. Shear back every few years to rejuvenate older plantings and remove woody stems.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or early fall; site in brighter light than typical ivy for best golden color.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, where new leaves emerge soft yellow-green and mature to a rich golden-buttercup yellow in brighter light; in deeper shade the foliage reverts toward green. Buttercup is a smaller-leaved, slower-growing selection than the species, making it easier to keep in bounds in beds, containers, and small-space groundcover plantings. Trailing stems root as they spread, so edge plantings to prevent it from climbing trees or structures. As with the species, confirm local invasive-species guidance before planting outdoors.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or early fall; grow in bright indirect light for the best variegation.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants in average, well-drained soil in partial shade, where small, triangular grey-green leaves are irregularly margined in creamy white. Glacier is a slower, more compact grower than the species, making it a popular choice for containers, hanging baskets, and small-scale groundcover where a less aggressive variegated ivy is wanted. Variegation is most pronounced with some bright indirect light; deep shade mutes the white margins toward plain grey-green. Trim back periodically to maintain dense, juvenile foliage and remove any reversion shoots of plain green growth before they take over.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or early fall; stem cuttings root readily in water or moist perlite.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where glossy, dark green leaves with distinctively curled and crimped margins give the foliage a ruffled, lace-like texture unlike any plain-leaved ivy. Ivalace is a compact, slow-to-moderate grower long favored among American Ivy Society reference cultivars for its dense, uniform habit in containers and small groundcover plantings. Its naturally tidy growth needs less frequent shearing than larger-leaved trailing types, though an occasional trim keeps older plantings from thinning at the center. As with other English ivy selections, check regional invasive-species status before planting outdoors.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or early fall; this is one of the most cold-hardy English ivy selections available.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where trailing stems root as they travel to form a dense, low evergreen mat. Baltic ivy has smaller leaves than the species and is among the most cold-hardy English ivy selections available, tolerating winters where straight species plants struggle; foliage often takes on a bronze-purple cast in cold weather and greens up again in spring. It is widely planted as a tough, low-maintenance groundcover on shaded banks and under trees in northern climates, though it carries the same invasive-species concerns as the species in much of the eastern United States. Shear back every few years to remove woody growth and renew dense cover.

common_name: Gold Child English Ivy (Gold-Margined Variegated Ivy)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or early fall; grow in some bright indirect light for the strongest gold variegation.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants in average, well-drained soil in partial shade, where small grey-green leaves are irregularly edged in creamy gold. Gold Child is a popular variegated groundcover and container ivy with a moderate, manageable growth rate between the more vigorous species and slower-growing compact cultivars. Gold margins develop most strongly with some bright indirect light; in deeper shade the variegation fades toward plain grey-green. Watch for and remove any all-green reversion shoots promptly, since they grow more vigorously than the variegated growth and can gradually overtake it.
